content: Royal Perth Hospital (RPH) is an 855-bed teaching hospital situated on the northeastern edge of the central business district of Perth, Western Australia. It also operates specialized rehabilitation facilities located in Shenton Park. The hospital's origins date back to June 1829, when the first colonial hospital was established in a tent on Garden Island, off the coast of Western Australia. By June 1830, the hospital tent was relocated to Cathedral Avenue in Perth. In 1833, a more permanent colonial hospital operated briefly from a rented room in a private house. In December 1840, the hospital reopened in a building that had previously served as stables, located at the corner of St Georges Terrace and Irwin Street. On July 14, 1855, the hospital began operations at its current site and was officially named the Colonial Hospital. Over the years, it underwent several name changes, becoming the Perth Public Hospital, then the Perth Hospital, and finally, in 1946, it was renamed Royal Perth Hospital. In 2005, the Western Australian Government announced plans to relocate Royal Perth Hospital's operations to a new, purpose-built facility in Murdoch, which would be named Fiona Stanley Hospital. Royal Perth Hospital is the largest hospital in Western Australia, employing over 6,000 staff and treating more than 70,000 patients annually. It offers a wide range of medical services, including imaging, cancer care, neurosciences, various surgical specialties, critical and emergency care, dermatology, internal medicine, hematology, and more. As a teaching hospital, RPH maintains strong affiliations with Western Australia's four major universities and TAFE institutions, providing practical and professional education opportunities. Notably, the hospital is home to a leading Burns Unit, which develops advanced technologies to aid in the rehabilitation of burn victims. The hospital is also a hub for medical research. Under the leadership of Professor Peter Leedman, RPH conducts extensive research into patient recovery and the optimization of staff practices. The hospital shares its campus with prominent research institutions, including the Western Australian Institute for Medical Research, facilitating numerous ongoing research projects. The hospital's researchers contribute significantly to international scientific literature, as evidenced by the publication of 158 articles and 114 abstracts in peer-reviewed medical, nursing, and scientific journals in 1998 alone. Additionally, RPH staff presented 190 papers at national and international professional conferences that year. The Royal Perth Rehabilitation Hospital, located in Shenton Park, was originally established as an isolation tent hospital during a smallpox outbreak in April 1893. Over the years, it has been known by various names, including the Isolation Hospital, the Victoria Hospital, and the Infectious Diseases Branch, before becoming the Royal Perth Rehabilitation Hospital. It gained prominence as a major rehabilitation center during the rehabilitation of polio patients following the epidemic of 1948–1956. Several distinguished medical professionals and researchers have been associated with Royal Perth Hospital. These include Dr. Fiona Wood, who was named Australian of the Year in 2005, and Professors Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, who were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005. The hospital's motto, Servio, reflects its commitment to service. Its logo, introduced in 1935, is based on the arms of the City of Perth and features St George's Cross on a white shield with a black swan in the top left corner, accompanied by a banner inscribed with the word Servio.
